scope: Research-only source-critical comparison of whole-genome transplantation compatibility barriers in Mollicutes and partial chromosome swapping in separately engineered Escherichia coli; original evidence/negative outcomes; no experiments

sources.citation: Labroussaa F, Lebaudy A, Baby V et al. Impact of donor–recipient phylogenetic distance on bacterial genome transplantation. Nucleic Acids Research 44:8501–8511 (2016).
sources.evidence_grade: E2 complete original publisher main Materials/Methods, Results, Discussion including Table 1, figures and rights; no supplementary raw sequencing or independent E3 reproduction
sources.rights: CC BY-NC 4.0; independent critical paraphrase only; no original figures, DNA sequences or extensive tables reproduced
sources.program: INRA/University of Bordeaux + University of Sherbrooke, one JCVI coauthor (Vashee)
sources.study_units: Three independent whole-genome transplantation experiments per species, four within-experiment transplantation events averaged; genotype check ten clones/species PCR and two PFGE+WGS; donor species are not independent founder cell origins
positive_observations: Six of seven tested Spiroplasma-group donor backgrounds yielded some directly prepared chromosome transfers into living M. capricolum including self-species control; five other donors succeeded
Mesoplasma florum is the most divergent successfully transplanted donor, from a separate genus, 92.47% shared identity across 79 core proteins in this original comparison
Donor-type colony phenotypes, PCR, chromosome PFGE and whole-genome sequences confirmed sampled full donor-genome transitions
All tested origin-of-replication plasmids including Spiroplasma citri origin replicated within recipient despite whole-chromosome transfer failure

key_numbers.source_table1_units: transplants/µg input genome DNA, mean ± SEM; source-reported for optimized donor concentrations
key_numbers.donor_source_volume_effect: ~2 µg DNA often maximized source-specific transfer, higher amounts lowered yields, mechanism unresolved

negative_results: Spiroplasma citri yielded no successful whole-genome transplants from bacteria or yeast; origin-bearing plasmid nonetheless replicated
Closely related Mycoplasma mycoides subsp mycoides transferred poorly from bacteria (~3.43±2.86/µg) and zero from yeast
Another donor Spiroplasma floricola was reported failure but no displayed direct dataset or denominator (data not shown)
Mesoplasma florum transferred poorly from bacteria 3.02±5.23 per µg with wide uncertainty, but successfully from yeast; source preparation matters
Phylogenetic distance confounded by larger genome and slower growth of Spiroplasma citri and by species-specific traits; no single direct causal mechanism proven
external_assistance: Donor bacterial cells and yeast intermediate for manipulation
Researchers constructed selective markers and performed PEG-mediated DNA introduction
Laboratory nutrients, culture/antibiotic selection, PCR and sequencing
sources.mechanistic_limit: Origin recognition insufficient for whole genome startup; cross genus Mollicutes not other class or abiotic boot

sources.citation: Baby V, Labroussaa F, Brodeur J et al. Cloning and Transplantation of the Mesoplasma florum Genome. ACS Synthetic Biology 7:209–217 (2018).
sources.evidence_grade: E1 original publisher/PubMed abstract and bibliographic metadata; full copyrighted publisher article available for purchase, final Methods/Results/supplement unavailable and not audited
sources.rights: Copyright © 2017 American Chemical Society. No verified open reuse license for full work; only short independent summary and bibliographic linking
sources.program: University of Sherbrooke + University of Bordeaux/INRA, shares several authors with P47-S1
positive_observations: Cloned Mesoplasma florum bacterial genome in living yeast
Transplanted Mesoplasma florum genome into living Mycoplasma capricolum
Whole-genome sequencing reportedly revealed some new variants in all sampled Mesoplasma transplants; fewer mutations in same-species M. capricolum->M. capricolum transplants
negative_results: Three researcher-performed successive transplantation rounds showed no reported difference in transplant efficiency
Specific genome mutation counts, phylogenetic sample denominators and functional effects unverified at abstract-only E1 depth
sources.experimental_units: Clone and sequence sample counts not established from original abstract; three successive investigator-run transfer rounds are not autonomous generations
external_assistance: Donor genome editing and researcher transplantation/selection
Prior shared Bordeaux/Sherbrooke project; not independent laboratory replication of 2016
sources.mechanistic_limit: Transferred DNA variants can be neutral or damaging and do not automatically imply novel selectable ecological benefit

sources.citation: Yoneji T, Fujita H, Mukai T, Su’etsugu M. Grand scale genome manipulation via chromosome swapping in Escherichia coli programmed by three one megabase chromosomes. Nucleic Acids Research 49:8407–8418 (2021).
sources.evidence_grade: E2 accessible complete original publisher main Materials/Methods, Results, Discussion, figures and rights; no E3 raw PFGE/source protocol recreation
sources.rights: CC BY 4.0 OUP 2021 main; no original figures/tables or data redistributed
sources.program: Rikkyo University (Japan), distinct from Mollicutes transplant teams
positive_observations: Viable engineered 3-Mb genome-reduced E. coli split into three approximately 1-Mb chromosomes with distinct origin and segregation elements
Two variants preserved three-chromosome pattern >100 generations of laboratory culture without antibiotic selection
Purified ~0.84-Mb and ~1.02-Mb circular chromosomes could be electroporated into living commercial competent E. coli in some conditions
Conjugation permitted replacement of portions of the multipartite chromosome set among viable engineered E. coli
negative_results: RGF138 grew about 2 times slower, RGF140 about 1.5 times slower, than viable DGF-298W parent
RGF140 frequently showed filamentous morphology and live/dead microscopy 53% versus RGF138 78%, parent 80%
Purified native-origin ~1.12-Mb ChrOri gave no electroporation colonies, despite swap by conjugation
ChrTer 6 intact among 110 antibiotic-resistant screened colonies, requiring PFGE/PCR to distinguish intact chromosome from resistance
Only two positive ChrLR recipient colonies from four commercial electroporation vials in a reported result
Own competent DGF-298-derived strain preparation was unsuccessful for 1-Mb chromosome transfer, unlike commercial cells
sources.experimental_units: Two engineered bacterial strain configurations from same reduced viable E coli starting chassis; >100 cultures generations not first-founder E3; cell microscopy viability percentages not count independent founder origins
external_assistance: Existing viable E. coli reduced-genome founder and lab culture
Researcher genetic splitting, plasmid selection, chromosome extraction, electroporation, conjugation and selection
Distinct replication/segregation origin modules from E coli F plasmid and Vibrio
Competent cells and externally prepared lab conditions
sources.conflicts_of_interest: Masayuki Su'etsugu disclosed co-founder, shareholder and chief scientific officer role at OriCiro Genomics, Inc. related to chromosome replication technology
sources.mechanistic_limit: Chromosome-part swap within viable cells is not complete whole-genome transplantation into dead cells, or de novo abiotic cellular reconstruction

reviewed_study_independence: P47-S1 and S2 share Bordeaux/Sherbrooke investigators and recipient chassis, and S1 includes a JCVI collaborator. P47-S3 is independent Rikkyo program but different chromosome swap endpoint. 3 primary papers are not 3 independent complete cell origin replications.
negative_evidence_scope: Bounded source and citation search did not find a separate independent author group directly repeating the 2026 inactivated-recipient Seidel assay with single-founder exclusions; absence from these sources does not prove absence from all literature.
cross_study_distinction: Full donor genome takeover of viable recipient vs partial chromosome swap within live engineered E coli
Whole chromosome boot versus small oriC plasmid replication
Live recipient vs genetically disabled recipient vs entirely inert nonliving origin
Genotype marker positive colony vs genome-wide donor identity vs observed functional self-maintaining descendants
Laboratory maintenance without antibiotic selection vs unattended ecological reproductive founding
release_gate: Reviewed exact-head PR workflow syntax/catalog/unittest success; no conflicting main/head movement before expected-head merge; independently successful resulting main push workflow
